statedReasoning: Per the důvodová zpráva (Obecná část, bod 1) of this poslanecký návrh by Mgr. Ing. Pavla Pivoňka Vaňková (submitted 1 July 2026, signed 1 July 2026 in Prague), the bill is a five-statute 'third pillar' interoperability package amending 586/1992 Sb. (daně z příjmů), 427/2011 Sb. (doplňkové penzijní spoření, DPS), 256/2004 Sb. (podnikání na kapitálovém trhu, governing the dlouhodobý investiční produkt, DIP), 262/2006 Sb. (zákoník práce) and 324/2025 Sb. (povinný příspěvek na produkty spoření na stáří). Its stated goal is to make retirement saving more advantageous by (1) letting time spent in DPS and DIP count cumulatively toward the 120-month tax-relief condition (Čl. I body 2-3, §15b); (2) allowing penalty-free partial transfers of up to 50% of participant+employer contributions (state contributions excluded) between DPS and DIP in both directions (§25a of 427/2011; §134ha of 256/2004); (3) a young-saver package: participants under 30, in their first 12 months of saving, get a state contribution of 50% of their monthly contribution (up to 1,000 Kč/month) instead of the standard ~20% subsidy — and, newly, this incentive is extended to DIP as well as DPS (§14 odst.3 of 427/2011; new §134l of 256/2004); (4) a mandatory 'life-cycle strategy' default plus a duty to warn savers who opt for conservative funds, replacing automatic de-risking near retirement with an opt-in, informed-choice model (§113a, §114 of 427/2011); (5) cutting the maximum performance fee pension companies may charge on 'ostatní účastnické fondy' from 15% to 10% of gains (§60 odst.4 of 427/2011), explicitly to narrow the cost gap with DIP; and (6) a brand-new zákoník práce right (§224a): an employee working at least half of standard weekly hours may request the employer match their own DPS/DIP contribution, and the employer must then pay at least 500 Kč/month once the employee proves they contribute at least 500 Kč/month themselves, with existing voluntary employer contributions counting toward the duty and a coordination rule (also written into 324/2025 §3 odst.5) that when this right overlaps the mandatory 324/2025 contribution for the same period, the employer pays only the higher of the two. Effective date is 1 January 2027. The DZ's RIA (bod 5) estimates the young-saver package at 600m-1.3bn Kč/year in net state cost, and separately models the new employer-match right: at a projected 70% take-up (~2.183m new recipients of ~3.119m eligible non-recipients), 'Scénář A' (employers absorb the cost without wage offsets) — which the DZ itself calls the more realistic outcome — shows private employers' gross costs rising 9.82bn Kč/year (7.76bn net after a 21% corporate-tax deduction) and public-sector employers' direct payroll costs rising 3.27bn Kč/year with no tax offset, for a combined net public-budget loss of 5.34bn Kč/year; the alternative 'Scénář B' (wage substitution) shows zero net cost to employers but a 5.91bn Kč/year loss to public budgets via foregone social/health contributions and personal income tax. The DZ separately claims employees below median income will see a 'significant improvement' in retirement provision from these measures, states there are no corruption-risk, privacy, or security impacts, and lists no identified lobbyists under the lobbying-disclosure law.
researchedContext: The amended statutes form the operational core of the Czech 'third pillar': 586/1992 Sb. is the income-tax code, 427/2011 Sb. governs doplňkové penzijní spoření (the pension-company-run successor to the older penzijní připojištění), 256/2004 Sb. is the capital-markets act under which the newer dlouhodobý investiční produkt (DIP, typically offered by banks/brokerages rather than pension companies) operates, 262/2006 Sb. is the labor code, and 324/2025 Sb. is a very recent (2025) law creating a mandatory retirement-savings contribution regime — this bill's own text states that, since 2026, payroll administrators must already handle a 4% mandatory pension contribution for employees in risk professions under that regime, though I did not independently fetch 324/2025's own text and cannot verify its full scope beyond what this bill's důvodová zpráva echoes. Substantively, the bill is best read as plumbing/interoperability work stitching DPS and DIP together (shared time-counting, bidirectional no-penalty transfers, parity in young-saver state support) plus one genuinely new entitlement — the employer-match right in the labor code — layered on top of the freshly enacted 324/2025 mandatory-contribution regime, with an explicit anti-duplication rule so employers do not pay both. I was not able to independently corroborate the DZ's cost/RIA figures (9.82bn / 7.76bn / 3.27bn / 5.34bn / 5.91bn Kč) against outside modelling, media coverage, or opposition/industry commentary — no such independent sourcing was fetched, so these numbers should be read as the sponsor's own estimates, not independently verified projections.

unstatedEffects.effect: The bill's own explanatory memorandum predicts the employer-match right will meaningfully help below-median-income employees, but the mechanism it creates (§224a odst.2 of the labor code) only obligates the employer once the employee has already proven they personally contribute at least 500 Kč/month to the same product. Workers with the least discretionary income are structurally the least able to self-fund that 500 Kč/month trigger, so the guaranteed beneficiaries of the new employer obligation skew toward employees who can already afford to save — in tension with the DZ's own distributional claim.
unstatedEffects.whoBenefits: Middle- and higher-income employees who can readily self-fund the 500 Kč/month trigger, and employers who already pay discretionary DPS/DIP contributions above that floor (credited automatically under odst.3, at no incremental cost to them).

unstatedEffects.effect: The DZ frames 'Scénář A' (no wage offset) as the realistic outcome of the new employer-match right, under which public budgets absorb a net 5.34bn Kč/year loss (3.27bn Kč in direct extra public-sector payroll costs plus 2.06bn Kč in foregone corporate tax from the 21% deduction private employers claim). In substance, a large share of the fiscal cost of what functions as tax-advantaged private-sector compensation restructuring is shifted onto the state budget and non-beneficiary taxpayers, a distributional consequence the RIA states as a bare number without framing it as a subsidy to employer compensation packages.
unstatedEffects.whoBenefits: Private employers (who get a 21%-CIT-shielded, state-subsidized way to reward employees) and the employees who receive the match as favorably-taxed income instead of ordinary wages; general taxpayers and public budgets absorb the offsetting loss.

unstatedEffects.effect: Cutting the maximum performance fee on 'ostatní účastnické fondy' from 15% to 10% (§60 odst.4 of 427/2011), while simultaneously extending state young-saver support to DIP for the first time and building explicit bidirectional, penalty-free transfer rails between DPS and DIP, structurally favors DIP providers (banks/brokerages, regulated under the capital-markets act) at the relative expense of penzijní společnosti (pension companies), whose product just had its profit-fee ceiling cut. The DZ frames this purely as pro-consumer cost convergence ('přiblíží DIP') without acknowledging the competitive/industry-structure shift it also produces.
unstatedEffects.whoBenefits: Banks and investment firms offering DIP products, which gain new client inflows, new bidirectional transfer pathways, and — for the first time — state-subsidized under-30 contributions, at the relative expense of pension companies' participant-fund fee revenue.

conflictAssessment: This is a clean-sponsor case, and the honest finding is the absence of a conflict rather than its presence. The bill is a single-MP poslanecký návrh (not a government bill), sponsored solely by Pavla Pivoňka Vaňková (STAN, Jihočeský kraj, MP since October 2021). Per the case-law graph's batch scan of this print (bill node bill:tisk:43370), zero sponsor-linked companies and 0 CZK of flagged public-contract value are recorded against this bill or its sponsor — a clean-hands profile matching the brief. Her public professional background, per Wikipedia and the Poslanecká sněmovna's own member record, is in secondary education, project/team management, and municipal public administration (head of internal affairs / deputy secretary, Lišov city office from 2014-2021) — not banking, pension administration, or capital-markets business, the sectors whose regulated entities (penzijní společnosti, DIP providers) stand to gain or lose fee revenue under this bill. No graph-recorded company, board seat, or public-contract tie connects her to a pension company, bank, or investment firm that this bill's fee-cap, portability, or employer-match provisions would benefit. The bill's real winners and losers identified above (DIP providers vs. pension companies; middle-income vs. lower-income employees able to self-fund the employer-match trigger; public budgets vs. private employers) are structural/systemic, not traceable to a named entity tied to the sponsor. Severity is assessed low: a real, non-trivial fiscal and distributional policy with legitimate technocratic critique available, but with no self-dealing, no undisclosed sponsor money tie, and a sponsor whose recorded profile and career background give no plausible personal-enrichment channel through this bill.
